newsitem.title: USA: Stocks off on profit taking; focus on Greenspan's testimony.
newsitem.headline: Stocks off on profit taking; focus on Greenspan's testimony.

text.p: Wall Street stocks fell Monday, still battling profit-taking in technology and big-name shares and nervous ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's congressional testimony Tuesday.
At 1 p.m. EDT (1700 GMT), the 30-stock Dow was off 4.41 points at 7,886.05 after losing 131 points in a broad-based sell-off Friday.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 2-1 on volume of 264 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq composite index, which is laced with technology shares, fell 10.76 points to 1,537.23.
"The market is still suffering from Friday's hangover," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "Breadth is very negative."
Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co., said: "The market is still consolidating. A lot of big-cap stocks, especially technology stocks, got ahead of themselves."

Last week, stocks rallied to record highs, with the Dow index zipping through the magic 8,000 level for the first time ever, then crumbled Friday when a drop in technology stocks triggered widespread profit-taking.
Tech stocks slid after Microsoft Corp. reported earnings which barely beat Wall Street estimates.
On Monday, stock markets were nervous, in case the same sort of thing happened when giant technology company International Business Machines Corp. reported its results.
IBM, due to post second-quarter earnings after the close, was expected to earn $1.42 per share vs. $1.26 in the year-ago quarter, according to a First Call analyst survey.
IBM, which managed to rise Friday despite a slump among high-tech stocks, was off 5/16 to 103-7/8.
Microsoft extended its losses, falling 4-1/2 to 136.
"Everybody wants those IBM numbers to come in as forecast," said Doug Meyers, vice president of equity trading at Interstate/Johnson Lane. "Traders hate surprises."

Financial markets were also on edge ahead of Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress Tuesday and Wednesday on the economy and monetary policy. Investors will be watching for statements on inflation and interest rates.

"With the market's decline on Friday and Greenspan's speech tomorrow, the stock market is nervous in here," said Ken Ducey, vice president and director of trading at BT Brokerage. "Sentiment is leaning to the sell side."

The Dow weighed the earnings from several of its 30-components, including Exxon Corp., which posted second-quarter earnings of 79 cents a share compared with 63 cents share a year ago and analysts' forecasts of 71 cents per share. Exxon gained 12/16 to 61-3/16.
But another Dow component, Boeing Co., fell 1-7/16 to 54-9/16 after reporting earnings of 48 cents per share vs. earnings of 68 cents a year earlier.
First Union Corp. shed 2-9/16 to 94-7/8, after it said it would buy Signet Banking Corp. in a stock swap valued at $3.25 billion. Signet's stock rose 13-14/16 to 50-9/16.
